summary: 'Human Adenovirus Vector Vaccine' is a vaccine-platform/class descriptor rather than a single defined product. These are recombinant vaccines that use a genetically modified, replication-deficient human adenovirus (for example serotype 5 [Ad5] or serotype 26 [Ad26]) as a vector to carry the gene for a target pathogen antigen (such as the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein) into host cells. The host cells then transiently express the antigen, eliciting both antibody and T-cell immune responses without the vector being able to replicate or cause infection. Well-known examples include adenovirus-vectored COVID-19 vaccines (e.g. Ad26.COV2.S and Ad5-based vaccines) and adenovirus-vectored Ebola vaccines; chimpanzee adenovirus vectors (e.g. ChAdOx1) are a related approach. Because indications, antigen, dose, schedule, contraindications and safety signals differ entirely by product, clinicians must consult the specific approved label/WHO product information for the individual vaccine in use. A rare safety signal of thrombosis with thrombocytopenia syndrome was associated with some adenoviral-vectored COVID-19 vaccines.

moa: A replication-deficient adenovirus is engineered by deleting genes (e.g. E1, often E3) required for viral replication and inserting the gene encoding a target pathogen antigen. After intramuscular injection the vector enters host cells and delivers the transgene to the nucleus, where the antigen is transcribed and translated. The expressed antigen is presented to the immune system, generating neutralising antibodies and antigen-specific CD4/CD8 T-cell responses, along with immune memory. The vector itself cannot replicate or cause adenoviral disease. Pre-existing immunity to the adenovirus serotype can reduce responses, which is why rarer human serotypes (e.g. Ad26) or non-human (chimpanzee) adenoviruses are sometimes used.
